2006年3月，Yuri Landman受噪音樂團Liars委託製琴；半年後完成: In March 2006 Yuri Landman was commissioned by the noise band Liars to build an instrument; half a year later two Moodswingers were finished, one for the guitarist and drummer Aaron Hemphill and one for himself. In 2008 the production model Moodswinger II came out. In 2009 he developed a derivative, the Home Swinger, for festival workshops, where participants built their own within four hours. In 2010 the Musical Instrument Museum in Phoenix added both models to its Dutch instrument-invention collection.
Moodswinger 是十二弦電齊特琴，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號: The Moodswinger is a twelve-string electric zither, Hornbostel–Sachs number 513. It was designed by Yuri Landman and has a movable third bridge that divides the strings into two segments, producing overtone polyphony; it has no frets and no real neck, and the pickup and electronics are mounted on the neck. The twelve strings are tuned round a circle of fourths, and the player uses the third bridge to locate the overtones. It was originally built for a noise band, with the designer and a member of the band each owning one.
Moodswinger 為十二弦電齊特琴，第三橋將每弦分成兩段，產生泛音多音。彈: The Moodswinger is a twelve-string electric zither, and the third bridge divides each string into two segments, producing overtone polyphony. When it is played you can hear three tones stacked: a soft attack tone, the corresponding overtone and a low fundamental. At most positions the attack tone and the overtone are the same note; at certain ratios they form a perfect fifth or a major third. The twelve strings are tuned round a circle of fourths, so every note of the equal-tempered scale can be played, and five adjacent strings and seven adjacent strings give a pentatonic scale and a major scale respectively. Unlike an ordinary electric guitar it has no frets and no real neck, and the pickup and electronics are built into the neck; the source does not say how the volume is controlled.

演奏時以手指撥弦，琴上印有音階作為移動第三橋與讀音的依據。第三橋將弦分成兩段，撥: The strings are plucked with the fingers, and a scale is printed on the instrument as a guide for moving the third bridge and reading the pitches. The third bridge divides the strings into two segments; plucking the side nearer the body produces overtones, and positions at simple integer ratios give clear overtones while more complex ones are indistinct. The twelve strings are tuned round a circle of fourths and divided into three groups of four; five adjacent strings give a pentatonic scale and seven a major scale, and choosing the right key avoids wrong notes. A beginner should first get used to the tuning, the fingerstyle and the position of the third bridge.
